extracted.intended_audience: parliamentarians, journalists, media regulators, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative principles for responsible reporting, broadcasting practice, and government/media conduct arising from the Hutton debate (e.g., libel/qualified privilege, accuracy, separation of fact/opinion, handling of intelligence). Useful for assessing media organisations, journalistic acts, and official communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence of qualified privilege (Reynolds principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where, on an issue of public importance, a newspaper or broadcaster makes defamatory allegations of fact that cannot be proved to be true, in some circumstances it is still not liable to pay damages for libel — the defence of qualified privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What circumstances give rise to that defence must be decided case-by-case; summarised by Lord Nicholls: 'The common law does not seek to set a higher standard than that of responsible journalism'. (References to Reynolds extracts and Lord Nicholls' speech cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for media: irresponsible journalism vs factual truth
rubrics_metrics.description: In assessing media conduct the central test is whether a broadcaster/newspaper was guilty of irresponsible journalism, not simply whether the allegations they broadcast or printed turned out to be untrue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus investigations and judgments on journalistic responsibility and procedure (checks, verification, handling of sources) rather than retrospective truth alone; protecting responsible reporting of matters of public importance is important even if alleged facts later prove false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness of reporters as a precondition for freedom on live programmes
rubrics_metrics.description: Live, unscripted programmes depend on giving reporters and presenters a good deal of freedom of action; the organisation must be able to trust its reporters before granting that freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial employers should vet reporters' reliability and maintain standards so that the latitude given for up-to-the-minute reporting does not lead to irresponsible broadcasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of news from comment/opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically a fundamental part of professional journalism was the separation of news reporting from the commentary and opinions expressed; mixing the two reduces public confidence and the value of the media's contribution to forming opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media organisations should reflect on re-establishing clearer boundaries and rigorous pre-publication checks; while not enforceable by law in all cases, mingling news and comment is identified as a harmful practice that 'leads ineluctably to' feuds and loss of respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imparting unwarranted certainty to intelligence-based documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents based almost exclusively on covert intelligence should not be presented with a degree of certainty which no such document can reasonably sustain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intelligence generally provides probabilities or possibilities, not certainty; drafters should avoid language that conveys undue certainty and should accurately reflect the underlying degree of confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for clear rules governing e-mail in government business
rubrics_metrics.description: E-mail has become a pervasive but unregulated form of communication that records exchanges but often sits outside formal procedural rules, blurring lines of authority and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish 'rules of the road' to bring e-mail communications within the ambit of other written communications (clarify authority, responsibility, retention, and procedural standing) to avoid confusion and diffused accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of accuracy and separation of fact and opinion in broadcasting (statutory requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasting and Television Act 1956 imposes a duty of accuracy and demands a separation of fact and opinion on radio and television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcasters are legally required to maintain accuracy and distinguish fact from opinion; this statutory duty underpins expectations about broadcast standards (note: does not cover print media).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public entitlement to greater information when the country is taken to war
rubrics_metrics.description: The public, when taken to war, is entitled to much more information than was given; the mystique of intelligence services should be dispelled to the extent compatible with necessary secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should aim for greater transparency about the basis for major decisions (subject to genuine security constraints) so that parliamentary and public scrutiny can be meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty: media must both report and, when justified, initiate news
rubrics_metrics.description: The media's purpose includes exposing important issues (e.g., deficiencies in government, humanitarian crises); programmes should continue to make news as well as report it rather than merely relaying government messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining investigative and challenging journalism is essential despite occasional mistakes; editorial organisations should avoid constraining themselves to passive reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional verification before public affirmation of allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: An organisation should verify original notes and evidence before publicly affirming and standing behind allegations made by individual journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporate responses to challenges (e.g., answering direct government questioning) require checking the underlying material; failure to do so undermines credibility (example: BBC's 'yes' reply without consulting Gilligan's original note).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unscripted/off-the-cuff reporting does not automatically excuse irresponsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'off the cuff' or unscripted may mitigate but does not absolve a journalist or broadcaster from responsibility for making serious allegations without adequate verification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While individual slips may be forgivable, subsequent editorial handling and institutional responses are crucial and can be far less forgivable if they fail to correct or investigate properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper handling of source identity and protection of individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about revealing the identity of sources or implicated individuals (e.g., naming Dr Kelly) require careful, planned processes to protect people and avoid ad hoc exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid improvised methods (described as an 'elaborate, and totally unprecedented 20-questions procedure') and instead have planned, coordinated approaches for protecting vulnerable individuals and handling disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of inquiries and publication of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Delays in publishing inquiries or reports (e.g., a year or more) are unconscionable; there is a prima facie case for timely reporting within a defined period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that investigations into matters of public importance are completed and published promptly so lessons can be acted upon and public confidence maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ministerial involvement and clear chains of authority in major decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Important decisions affecting departments (e.g., defence-related decisions) should involve the responsible minister and follow clear lines of authority and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid decisions being taken without the responsible minister present or without clear accountability; blurred decision-making undermines governance and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media independence: resist governmental pressure and preserve fearless scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC (and media generally) must resist pressure from governments and preserve independence to question, probe, and reveal errors—their duty is not to relay government messages uncritically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policymakers should be cautious in attempts to curb or reshape media organisations; public support for independent media is a factor to consider (e.g., licence renewal debates).
